passage: Come, Deepak, sit by your Darshan Dada. You want to know how to help your friend? Let me tell you about Suresh. We were twenty, sharing a room in the college hostel, when his father's shop burned down. Suresh stopped going to class and lay facing the wall. I wanted to give him speeches. I even started to say, "When my mother died, I..." and stopped, because it wasn't about me. So I did small things. I brought his dinner from the mess. I sat on the floor with my books while he stared at the wall. Every evening I asked, "Walk to the tea stall?" Most days he said no. Some days, yes. After a month I told him, "I'm your friend, not a doctor. There's a doctor at the college clinic who talks with students. I'll come with you." He went. Fifty years later, Suresh still sends me mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What happened to Suresh's father's shop?
qa.a: It burned down.

qa.q: Why did Darshan stop in the middle of saying "When my mother died"?
qa.a: Dada caught himself, uneasy that comparing his own pain would make it about himself rather than Suresh.

qa.q: What choice did Dada make after a month?
qa.a: He admitted he was a friend, not a doctor, and offered to go with Suresh to the doctor at the college clinic.

qa.q: What might Dada's quiet company have meant to Suresh?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt he was not alone and not pressured, which made it easier to accept the tea-stall walks and later the clinic.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he helped a struggling friend he shared a hostel room with by listening, keeping him company and bringing food, not lecturing or comparing pain, and nudging him to a doctor.

passage: Gurleen's own exams started on Monday, and the hostel wifi kept dropping. Still, every night at ten she called her friend Chaitanya in his city three hundred kilometres away, even if only for five minutes. Since he'd failed his second-year paper, he mostly spoke in short, flat sentences. On Wednesday he said, "Everyone else is moving on and I'm stuck." Gurleen felt a sharp flicker of resentment. She had her own paper in nine hours. Then she heard how tired he sounded and let it go. She didn't tell him about her cousin who had failed and bounced back, and she didn't list study tips. She only said, "That sounds really heavy. I'm here." On Thursday she found the number for his college counselling cell and sent it with one line: "I'm not a counsellor, but these people are. Want me to stay on the call while you book?" He did. The booking took four minutes.

qa.q: At what time did Gurleen call Chaitanya every night?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen feel a flicker of resentment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Her own paper was in nine hours, and she was tired and stretched by giving time she needed.

qa.q: What choice did Gurleen make on Thursday, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She sent the counselling cell's number and offered to stay on the call while Chaitanya booked, a small practical step toward professional help.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt hearing "That sounds really heavy. I'm here" instead of study tips?
qa.a: He may have felt heard rather than judged, which made him more willing to book the counsellor.

grounding: It shows a friend in exam week checking in daily, listening without comparing or lecturing, and giving a small practical nudge toward professional care.

passage: After Nandini failed her accountancy exam, she stopped coming to the Pune library where they always studied. Saurabh didn't send a speech. He sent, "Chai at six? You don't have to talk." She came, hood up, and said almost nothing. He didn't tell her about the time he'd failed maths, or say "at least you can retake it." He just listened when she finally spoke. After that he texted every evening, "How was today, 1 to 10?" On Sunday he helped her carry her laundry to the dhobi. When she said she felt stuck in her own head, he said, "I'm not the right person to untangle that, but the college counsellor is good. Want me to walk over with you on Monday?" She nodded.

qa.q: What did Saurabh text Nandini every evening?
qa.a: "How was today, 1 to 10?"

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when Saurabh said she didn't have to talk?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved and less pressured, able to be with a friend without explaining herself.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that shows being present without fixing?
qa.a: He listened without lecturing or comparing, checked in daily, helped with laundry and nudged her toward the college counsellor.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt as a supporter, knowing his limits?
qa.a: He probably felt caring but realistic, knowing he was not a counsellor and that she needed more than a friend.

grounding: Shows a friend who listens, checks in regularly, offers company and small practical help without lecturing or comparing pain, and nudges toward professional care.

passage:
"Tushar, I brought samosas. And the notes from Tuesday."
"You didn't have to."
"I wanted to. How are you doing, really?"
"Honestly? Since Papa lost his job, I can't focus. I just feel heavy all the time."
"That sounds exhausting." Elizabeth sat on the floor. She didn't say, "Cheer up," or, "My family had it worse last year."
"You're not going to tell me to be positive?"
"Nope. I'm just going to sit here and eat samosas with you."
Tushar laughed a little. "Thanks."
"Can I say one thing, though? I'm your friend, not a counsellor. The student centre has people who are good at this. I'll come with you."
"Maybe. Let me think."
"Take your time. I'll text you tomorrow either way."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth bring Tushar?
qa.a: Samosas and the notes from Tuesday.

qa.q: How is Tushar feeling since Papa lost the job?
qa.a: Tushar feels heavy and unable to focus, weighed down all the time.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth's support wise?
qa.a: She listened, didn't lecture or compare, offered company and practical help, accepted she isn't a counsellor and gently suggested the student centre.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel sitting with Tushar?
qa.a: She probably feels caring and steady, content to be present without needing to fix things.

grounding: Shows a friend who listens, offers company and small practical help without lecturing or comparing pain, and gently nudges toward professional care.

passage: Last year, when Baljeet went quiet after his parents' divorce, I thought my job was to fix him. I'm Nilesh, and I kept sending him videos about positive thinking and telling him about my own bad year. He stopped replying. So I changed. I just texted "thinking of you" every couple of days, and "want to walk to the canal?" on Sundays. I brought him food when he forgot to eat, and I shut up and listened when he talked. Once he snapped at me, and I didn't take it personally. After a few weeks I said, "I care about you, but I'm not a therapist. Would you see someone?" He did. Now he says those Sunday walks mattered more than all my advice.

qa.q: What did Nilesh invite Baljeet to do on Sundays?
qa.a: To walk to the canal.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel on realising the fixing approach wasn't working?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt frustrated and worried when Baljeet stopped replying, which led to a change of approach.

qa.q: What change made Nilesh's support work?
qa.a: Nilesh stopped lecturing and comparing, checked in regularly, offered company and food, listened and nudged Baljeet toward a therapist.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see those Sunday walks now?
qa.a: Baljeet says the walks mattered more than all of Nilesh's advice.

grounding: Shows a friend who stops lecturing and comparing pain, and instead listens, checks in, offers company and small help, then nudges toward professional care.

passage:
Warden's note, women's hostel, second floor.
This term I've watched Kalyani look after her friend Urmila, who has been struggling since her grandmother died. Kalyani doesn't lecture. She never says "at least" or "I went through worse." She sits on the end of Urmila's bed in the evenings, sometimes talking, sometimes just doing her own homework beside her.
She brings Urmila's lab notes back from class and makes sure there's a plate of rice waiting after mess hours. She knocks every morning to check in.
Last week Urmila snapped, "Stop hovering, you're not my mother." Kalyani looked hurt and left. But she came back the next evening anyway, with tea.
Yesterday Kalyani came to me. "I'm not a counsellor. I think she needs someone trained." We agreed she would suggest it gently to Urmila. This morning Urmila asked me for the campus counsellor's number.

qa.q: What does Kalyani make sure is waiting after mess hours?
qa.a: A plate of rice.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when Urmila told her to stop hovering?
qa.a: She felt hurt and stung, and left, but her care won out and she came back the next evening with tea.

qa.q: Which parts of Kalyani's support worked well?
qa.a: Listening, checking in, keeping Urmila company, practical help with notes and food, no lectures or comparing pain, and recognising she isn't a therapist so she nudged Urmila toward professional care.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about Kalyani's evening visits?
qa.a: She may sometimes feel crowded or resentful, but also less alone and cared for, which helped her ask for the counsellor.

grounding: A warden observes Kalyani listening, checking in, offering company and practical help without lecturing, and nudging her grieving friend toward professional care.
